newsitem.title: GERMANY: PHILIPS WANTS OUT OF GRUNDIG CONTRACT.
newsitem.headline: PHILIPS WANTS OUT OF GRUNDIG CONTRACT.

text.p: Dutch electronics giant Philips N.V. wants to dissolve its remaining contractual obligations to loss-ridden Grundig AG [GRNG.CN], Philips' chief financial officer said.

In an interview with the Sueddeutsche Zeitung published on Wednesday, Dudley Eustace said Philips wants to dissolve the pact with the Max Grundig Foundation under which it pays 45 million marks a year to the Grundig family heirs, the passive majority shareholders in the company.
The pact, which gave Philips control of the company despite its minority stake, would also have Philips buy the 68 percent of Grundig it does not already own in 2004 for 540 million marks.
At one point Eustace indicated the contract to purchase the remaining stock was an option, but at another point he termed it an obligation.
In either case, Philips wants out.
"We want to end our obligation to buy the remaining 68.4 percent of the stock," Eustace said, adding that negotiations were under way. "We don't know what the family wants."
Last year Philips said it would no longer cover Grundig's losses, and in January it said it would scale back its role to that of an ordinary minority shareholder.
Eustace said he had no hard estimate of Grundig's current value, but that it was debt-free.
"It is in business and it has a very valuable brand-name," he said.

Eustace rejected criticism that Philips had plundered Grundig, saying Philips invested 1.5 million marks in Grundig in its 12-years at the helm, and will also cover the 1996 losses Grundig estimates at 350 million marks.
"We are not taking a pfennig away from Grundig," he said.
Eustace stressed that Philips remains a partner at Grundig, not just in its capital but as a major parts supplier.
The future of this cooperation will depend on Grundig's new partner.
Eustace said the weak market for consumer electronics and the high cost of manufacturing in Germany were to blame for Grundig's woes.
"Either one gets out of the business or one moves to countries with low costs," he said.
